I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad

Threat.value: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Memory.value: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
I feel isolated and set apart from others
I can't stop bad things from happening to me

issues.item: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: Contamination/feeling dirty is much more characteristic of sexual trauma than a mugging/robbery. In a robbery case it is not impossible, but without any corroborating interpersonal violation, bodily disgust, or related threat/memory content, this item is clinically hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Emotional Closeness: Someone getting emotionally close to me
issues.explanation: Emotional closeness as a trigger is difficult to link to the stated trauma type of mugging/robbery and to the rest of the profile. The other triggers, threat items, and memory content point to danger/safety and coercion themes, whereas this item implies an intimacy/interpersonal-betrayal theme that is not represented elsewhere.

vignette: Aisha is a 22-year-old South Asian woman who works as a delivery driver. She has been experiencing significant distress following a mugging that occurred six months ago when she was delivering packages in a less populated area of the city late one evening. A man approached her from behind and forced her out of her vehicle, threatening to harm her if she resisted. The sheer loss of autonomy, combined with the immediate presence of an authority figure-she remembers seeing a police car nearby that did nothing-left her feeling both helpless and isolated. Since the incident, Aisha has developed a profound fear of driving or even being a passenger in any vehicle. She recalls how the mugging was precipitated by her inability to escape quickly enough and now constantly worries about potential threats on the road. This fear has led her to avoid driving altogether, resulting in significant occupational consequences. Her job performance has suffered because she often misses delivery deadlines or skips routes entirely. In an attempt to cope with her intense anxiety, Aisha has started using recreational drugs. She finds that these substances provide a temporary escape from the persistent feeling of being under threat. However, this maladaptive coping mechanism has not resolved her underlying fears and has instead exacerbated her sense of isolation and guilt for not taking better care of herself. Aisha tells herself that the mugging did not really happen or was not as bad as she remembers it to be. This magical thinking provides a brief respite from the overwhelming emotions, but it does little to alleviate the intrusive memories that plague her mind. She experiences intense emotional reactions without clear visual imagery-often feeling the fear and panic of that night without being able to conjure specific images. Additionally, auditory recall haunts her; she hears snippets of what was said during the mugging, which brings back vivid sensations of terror. The memory of the traumatic event is fragmented into a series of snapshots in her mind: the initial approach by the mugger, the feeling of powerlessness when he forced her out of the car, and the desperate look on his face as she handed over her belongings. These images are disjointed but incredibly vivid in their emotional intensity. Aisha's threat monitoring is relentless. She always identifies escape routes wherever she goes and wakes up multiple times during the night to check if everything is secure. Despite these precautions, she remains unable to relax even when she knows she is safe, perpetually on edge as if another threat could arise at any moment. The negative appraisals that Aisha holds are deeply ingrained. She feels a profound sense of guilt for not doing more to prevent the mugging and believes that she will never forgive herself. Her experiences have reinforced her belief in her own helplessness, making it difficult for her to trust in her ability to protect herself from future harm. These symptoms have taken a significant toll on Aisha's life. She has distanced herself from friends and family, feeling that they cannot understand what she is going through. The constant state of alertness and avoidance has left her feeling exhausted and overwhelmed. It was the mounting pressure at work and the realization that her coping mechanisms were no longer sustainable that finally brought her to seek help. Aisha is most afraid of never being able to feel safe again, but she also hopes for a future where she can regain control over her life and find some measure of peace. She seeks therapy in the hope of understanding and managing her reactions so that she can reclaim her sense of autonomy and trust in herself.
